knowledge_point.title: Expressing a Line Integral Along a Circular Path as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem

question.:question/problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}4{y}^{2}\,dx+4x\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation? Use $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, and simplify the integrand pointwise before integration.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/published-probe/17592186176024/17592186176024/circle-6.png)

Since $P(x,y)=4{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=4x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} &=8y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}4{y}^{2}\,dx+4x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4-8y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4-8y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(4-8\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}4r-8{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
